Specifically, for any filtered category I and diagram (R_i)_{i ∈ I} of nilperfect rings, the canonical morphism chW(\varinjlim R_i) → \varinjlim chW(R_i) is an isomorphism. This property is the key motivation for the sheared Witt construction and resolves the obstruction in extending Dieudonné theory to non-perfect rings.

concept.lean_guess: The conjecture follows from verifying that the pullback defining chW(R) commutes with filtered colimits. Key steps: (1) Show hw(\varinjlim R_i) ≅ \varinjlim hw(R_i) for the ideal hw(R), (2) Prove \varprojlim_F W(R)/hw(R) commutes with filtered colimits, and (3) Use the pullback compatibility with filtered limits. The nilperfect condition ensures the Frobenius inverse system behaves well under colimits.

## 1. The reciprocal-root symmetry

For a monic characteristic polynomial `π(X)` of degree `q` with `π(0) ≠ 0`, the
reversed polynomial `X^q · π(1/X)` has as roots exactly the reciprocals of the
roots of `π`.

Example: `π(X) = X^3 − X^2 − X − 1` (Tribonacci), roots `≈ 1.8393, −0.4196 ± 0.6063i`.

growth rates. This asymmetry is what forces coincidence sets to be finite.

Each conjecture below is bold, falsifiable, and derived from the findings of this
research cycle on large common values of an ABC recurrence pair and its reciprocal.

## Conjecture 1 — Two is sharp, and attained

For every integer q > 3 there exist admissible generalized ABC data whose
recurrence pair (a_n), (b_m) achieves exactly two common values above every
effective threshold, and no admissible data achieves three.

The key insight is that the coincidence a_n = b_m is governed by an S-unit
equation in the multiplicative group generated by the reciprocal dominant roots,
and such equations carry a rigid two-dimensional solution geometry that caps the
number of large solutions at two while permitting that maximum to be realized.

Why now? The reduction from counting coincident indices to counting coincident
values is now settled, so the entire difficulty concentrates in a single, sharply
posed extremal question about S-unit solution counts, which recent effective
methods in the theory of linear forms in logarithms are strong enough to attack.

## Conjecture 2 — Reciprocal growth dichotomy forces finiteness

Whenever a recurrence and its reciprocal each have a unique dominant root and
those two dominant roots are multiplicatively independent, the set of common
values is finite, with a bound depending only on the degree and the height of the
defining data.

The key insight is that coefficient reversal inverts the roots, so a dominant root
larger than one becomes the smallest root of the reciprocal; the resulting mismatch
in growth rates makes exact equality of the two sequences a measure-zero
coincidence that transcendence theory can bound.

Why now? The exact duality between coefficient reversal and root inversion has been
pinned down cleanly, giving a precise handle on the two growth rates and turning a
vague "different speeds" intuition into a quantitative separation.

## Conjecture 3 — Collapse only through multiplicative dependence

The only way for an ABC recurrence pair to share infinitely many values is for the
two dominant roots to be multiplicatively dependent; equivalently, the coincidence
set is infinite precisely when one sequence is, up to a fixed shift and scaling, a
subsequence of the other.

The key insight is that infinite coincidence forces a nontrivial multiplicative
relation between the dominant roots, mirrored at the elementary level by the fact
that powers of two and powers of three meet only at one, because two and three are
multiplicatively independent.

Why now? The clean elementary model — coprime bases never share large powers — has
been isolated and proved, providing a template for the general dichotomy and a
concrete degenerate case to test any proposed classification against.

import Mathlib

/-!
# γ-positivity of symmetric (palindromic) polynomials

This file develops the elementary theory of **γ-positivity** for real polynomials,
the exact algebraic property appearing in the study of Ehrhart `h*`-polynomials of
symmetric edge polytopes.

For a degree parameter `n`, the *γ-basis* of the space of polynomials that are
symmetric about `n/2` is
`{ t^i (1+t)^(n-2i) : 0 ≤ i ≤ ⌊n/2⌋ }`.
A polynomial `p` is **γ-positive of order `n`** if it is a nonnegative real
combination of these basis elements.

The main results here:

* `gammaBasis_coeff` — closed form for the coefficients of a basis element in terms
  of binomial coefficients;
* `gammaBasis_palindromic` — each basis element is palindromic about `n/2`;
* `IsGammaPositive.palindromic` — **γ-positivity implies palindromicity** (symmetry
  of the coefficient sequence), the structural constraint underlying every
  `h*`-polynomial of a symmetric edge polytope;
* `IsGammaPositive.coeff_nonneg` — γ-positive polynomials have nonnegative
  coefficients.

## Reference frame

The catalog entries `ohsugi-tsuchiya-conj`, `higashitani-jochemko-michalek`, `gal`
and `branden-gamma` concern precisely the γ-positivity of these Ehrhart
`h*`-polynomials; the phenomenon that palindromicity is *necessary but not
sufficient* for γ-positivity is what makes the "minimal dimension 36" question
nontrivial (see `GammaPositivityCounterexample.lean`).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): γ-positivity is a strict strengthening of palindromicity;
every γ-positive polynomial is palindromic and has nonnegative, unimodal coefficients,
but the converse fails already in very small degree.
Experiment (Experimenter): computed the coefficient vectors of `t^i(1+t)^(n-2i)` for
small `n`; each is a shifted binomial row, symmetric about `n/2`.
Analysis (Analyst): the symmetry `C(n-2i,k-i)=C(n-2i,(n-2i)-(k-i))` is the engine;
nonnegativity is immediate; unimodality needs the same-center superposition argument.
Critique (Critic): must guard `k ≤ n` for palindromicity, else Nat subtraction
`n - k` collapses to `0` and the identity is false.
Synthesis: the coefficient formula `gammaBasis_coeff` reduces both structural
theorems to binomial identities.
-/

namespace GammaPositivity

open Polynomial BigOperators

/-- The `i`-th element of the γ-basis in order `n`: `t^i (1+t)^(n-2i)`. -/
noncomputable def gammaBasis (n i : ℕ) : ℝ[X] := (1 + X) ^ (n - 2 * i) * X ^ i

/-- Closed form for the coefficients of a γ-basis element. -/
theorem gammaBasis_coeff (n i k : ℕ) :
    (gammaBasis n i).coeff k =
      if i ≤ k then ((n - 2 * i).choose (k - i) : ℝ) else 0 := by
  unfold gammaBasis
  rw [Polynomial.coeff_mul_X_pow']
  simp only [Polynomial.coeff_one_add_X_pow]


/-- The coefficients of a γ-basis element are nonnegative. -/
theorem gammaBasis_coeff_nonneg (n i k : ℕ) : 0 ≤ (gammaBasis n i).coeff k := by
  rw [gammaBasis_coeff]
  split
  · exact_mod_cast Nat.zero_le _
  · exact le_refl 0

/-- Each γ-basis element is palindromic about `n/2`: its coefficient sequence is
symmetric under `k ↦ n - k` for `k ≤ n`, provided `2 i ≤ n`. -/
theorem gammaBasis_palindromic (n i k : ℕ) (h2 : 2 * i ≤ n) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    (gammaBasis n i).coeff k = (gammaBasis n i).coeff (n - k) := by
  rw [gammaBasis_coeff, gammaBasis_coeff]
  by_cases hik : i ≤ k
  · by_cases hik2 : i ≤ n - k
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_true]
      have hkm : k - i ≤ n - 2 * i := by omega
      have hrw : n - k - i = (n - 2 * i) - (k - i) := by omega
      rw [hrw, Nat.choose_symm hkm]
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_true, if_false]
      rw [Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt (by omega)]; simp
  · by_cases hik2 : i ≤ n - k
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_false, if_true]
      rw [Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt (by omega)]; simp
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_false]

/-- A polynomial is **γ-positive of order `n`** if it is a nonnegative real
combination of the γ-basis elements `t^i (1+t)^(n-2i)` for `0 ≤ i ≤ ⌊n/2⌋`. -/
def IsGammaPositive (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ[X]) : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : ℕ → ℝ, (∀ i, 0 ≤ γ i) ∧
    p = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (n / 2 + 1), C (γ i) * gammaBasis n i

/-- A polynomial is **palindromic of order `n`** if its coefficient sequence is
symmetric under `k ↦ n - k` on `{0, …, n}`. -/
def IsPalindromic (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ[X]) : Prop := ∀ k ≤ n, p.coeff k = p.coeff (n - k)

/-- **γ-positivity implies palindromicity.** This is the structural symmetry shared
by every Ehrhart `h*`-polynomial of a symmetric edge polytope. -/
theorem IsGammaPositive.palindromic {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ[X]} (hp : IsGammaPositive n p) :
    IsPalindromic n p := by
  obtain ⟨γ, hγ, rfl⟩ := hp
  intro k hk
  rw [Polynomial.finset_sum_coeff, Polynomial.finset_sum_coeff]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro i hi
  rw [Polynomial.coeff_C_mul, Polynomial.coeff_C_mul]
  have hin : 2 * i ≤ n := by
    simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hi; omega
  rw [gammaBasis_palindromic n i k hin hk]

/-- γ-positive polynomials have nonnegative coefficients. -/
theorem IsGammaPositive.coeff_nonneg {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ[X]} (hp : IsGammaPositive n p)
    (k : ℕ) : 0 ≤ p.coeff k := by
  obtain ⟨γ, hγ, rfl⟩ := hp
  rw [Polynomial.finset_sum_coeff]
  apply Finset.sum_nonneg
  intro i _
  rw [Polynomial.coeff_C_mul]
  exact mul_nonneg (hγ i) (gammaBasis_coeff_nonneg n i k)

end GammaPositivity

# γ-positivity of symmetric (palindromic) polynomials

This file develops the elementary theory of **γ-positivity** for real polynomials,
the exact algebraic property appearing in the study of Ehrhart `h*`-polynomials of
symmetric edge polytopes.

For a degree parameter `n`, the *γ-basis* of the space of polynomials that are
symmetric about `n/2` is
`{ t^i (1+t)^(n-2i) : 0 ≤ i ≤ ⌊n/2⌋ }`.
A polynomial `p` is **γ-positive of order `n`** if it is a nonnegative real
combination of these basis elements.

* `gammaBasis_coeff` — closed form for the coefficients of a basis element in terms
  of binomial coefficients;
* `gammaBasis_palindromic` — each basis element is palindromic about `n/2`;
* `IsGammaPositive.palindromic` — **γ-positivity implies palindromicity** (symmetry
  of the coefficient sequence), the structural constraint underlying every
  `h*`-polynomial of a symmetric edge polytope;
* `IsGammaPositive.coeff_nonneg` — γ-positive polynomials have nonnegative
  coefficients.

and `branden-gamma` concern precisely the γ-positivity of these Ehrhart
`h*`-polynomials; the phenomenon that palindromicity is *necessary but not
sufficient* for γ-positivity is what makes the "minimal dimension 36" question
nontrivial (see `GammaPositivityCounterexample.lean`).

every γ-positive polynomial is palindromic and has nonnegative, unimodal coefficients,
but the converse fails already in very small degree.

`n - k` collapses to `0` and the identity is false.

namespace GammaPositivity

open Polynomial BigOperators

/-- The `i`-th element of the γ-basis in order `n`: `t^i (1+t)^(n-2i)`. -/
noncomputable def gammaBasis (n i : ℕ) : ℝ[X] := (1 + X) ^ (n - 2 * i) * X ^ i

/-- Closed form for the coefficients of a γ-basis element. -/
theorem gammaBasis_coeff (n i k : ℕ) :
    (gammaBasis n i).coeff k =
      if i ≤ k then ((n - 2 * i).choose (k - i) : ℝ) else 0 := by
  unfold gammaBasis
  rw [Polynomial.coeff_mul_X_pow']
  simp only [Polynomial.coeff_one_add_X_pow]


/-- The coefficients of a γ-basis element are nonnegative. -/
theorem gammaBasis_coeff_nonneg (n i k : ℕ) : 0 ≤ (gammaBasis n i).coeff k := by
  rw [gammaBasis_coeff]
  split
  · exact_mod_cast Nat.zero_le _
  · exact le_refl 0

/-- Each γ-basis element is palindromic about `n/2`: its coefficient sequence is
symmetric under `k ↦ n - k` for `k ≤ n`, provided `2 i ≤ n`. -/
theorem gammaBasis_palindromic (n i k : ℕ) (h2 : 2 * i ≤ n) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    (gammaBasis n i).coeff k = (gammaBasis n i).coeff (n - k) := by
  rw [gammaBasis_coeff, gammaBasis_coeff]
  by_cases hik : i ≤ k
  · by_cases hik2 : i ≤ n - k
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_true]
      have hkm : k - i ≤ n - 2 * i := by omega
      have hrw : n - k - i = (n - 2 * i) - (k - i) := by omega
      rw [hrw, Nat.choose_symm hkm]
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_true, if_false]
      rw [Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt (by omega)]; simp
  · by_cases hik2 : i ≤ n - k
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_false, if_true]
      rw [Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt (by omega)]; simp
    · simp only [hik, hik2, if_false]

/-- A polynomial is **γ-positive of order `n`** if it is a nonnegative real
combination of the γ-basis elements `t^i (1+t)^(n-2i)` for `0 ≤ i ≤ ⌊n/2⌋`. -/
def IsGammaPositive (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ[X]) : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : ℕ → ℝ, (∀ i, 0 ≤ γ i) ∧
    p = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range (n / 2 + 1), C (γ i) * gammaBasis n i

/-- A polynomial is **palindromic of order `n`** if its coefficient sequence is
symmetric under `k ↦ n - k` on `{0, …, n}`. -/
def IsPalindromic (n : ℕ) (p : ℝ[X]) : Prop := ∀ k ≤ n, p.coeff k = p.coeff (n - k)

/-- **γ-positivity implies palindromicity.** This is the structural symmetry shared
by every Ehrhart `h*`-polynomial of a symmetric edge polytope. -/
theorem IsGammaPositive.palindromic {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ[X]} (hp : IsGammaPositive n p) :
    IsPalindromic n p := by
  obtain ⟨γ, hγ, rfl⟩ := hp
  intro k hk
  rw [Polynomial.finset_sum_coeff, Polynomial.finset_sum_coeff]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro i hi
  rw [Polynomial.coeff_C_mul, Polynomial.coeff_C_mul]
  have hin : 2 * i ≤ n := by
    simp only [Finset.mem_range] at hi; omega
  rw [gammaBasis_palindromic n i k hin hk]

/-- γ-positive polynomials have nonnegative coefficients. -/
theorem IsGammaPositive.coeff_nonneg {n : ℕ} {p : ℝ[X]} (hp : IsGammaPositive n p)
    (k : ℕ) : 0 ≤ p.coeff k := by
  obtain ⟨γ, hγ, rfl⟩ := hp
  rw [Polynomial.finset_sum_coeff]
  apply Finset.sum_nonneg
  intro i _
  rw [Polynomial.coeff_C_mul]
  exact mul_nonneg (hγ i) (gammaBasis_coeff_nonneg n i k)

end GammaPositivity

## 2. Solving the γ-systems (counterexample hunt)

We test the universal claim "palindromic ⇒ γ-positive" on small palindromic targets.

**Target `1 + t^2` (order 2).** Writing `1 + t^2 = γ₀ B_{2,0} + γ₁ B_{2,1}`:
- coeff `t^0`: `γ₀ = 1`
- coeff `t^1`: `2γ₀ + γ₁ = 0 ⟹ γ₁ = -2 < 0`.

**Target `1 + t + t^2 + t^3 + t^4` (order 4).** Writing it as `Σ γ_i B_{4,i}`:
- coeff `t^0`: `γ₀ = 1`
- coeff `t^1`: `4γ₀ + γ₁ = 1 ⟹ γ₁ = -3 < 0`.

This is the degree-4 shadow of the "minimal dimension 36" phenomenon: every *necessary*
consequence of γ-positivity (nonnegativity, symmetry, unimodality) can hold while
γ-positivity fails.

**Positive control `(1+t)^n`.** `γ₀ = 1`, all other `γ_i = 0` — γ-positive for all `n`.

- Sums of order-`n` γ-positive polynomials are γ-positive (add γ-vectors). Verified.

The γ-basis rows are binomial coefficients (OEIS A007318, Pascal's triangle).

cone structure) rather than the full graph-theoretic classification.

# Future Directions

## 1. Unimodality is not enough: the persistent gamma-gap of flat symmetric sequences

**Conjecture.** For every degree `n ≥ 2`, the all-ones symmetric polynomial
`1 + t + t^2 + ⋯ + t^n` — which is palindromic, nonnegative, and unimodal — fails to be
gamma-positive, and its gamma-expansion forces the second gamma-coefficient to equal
`1 − n`, growing more negative without bound as the degree increases.

The key insight is that gamma-positivity is governed by a *triangular* change of basis
whose second coordinate reads off `c_1 − n·c_0`; whenever the leading coefficients are
comparable, this quantity is negative, so gamma-positivity fails even though every one of
its classical necessary conditions (symmetry, nonnegativity, unimodality) holds. This
separates gamma-positivity strictly from unimodality already in the smallest nontrivial
degrees.

**Why now?** The smallest palindromic, unimodal, nonnegative sequences that are not
gamma-positive can now be pinned down exactly, turning a qualitative "necessary but not
sufficient" folklore statement into a sharp, computable degree-by-degree obstruction.

## 2. The graded cone of gamma-positive polynomials and its extreme rays

**Conjecture.** The gamma-positive polynomials of each order form a convex cone whose
extreme rays are precisely the basis elements `t^i (1+t)^{n−2i}`, and the family of these
cones, glued together by the multiplication law
`t^i(1+t)^{m−2i} · t^j(1+t)^{n−2j} = t^{i+j}(1+t)^{(m+n)−2(i+j)}`,
forms a graded commutative cone-semiring in which factorization into irreducible
gamma-positive pieces is unique.

The key insight is that multiplying two of these building blocks *adds their indices*,
so gamma-positivity behaves exactly like nonnegativity of coefficients in a graded
polynomial ring: closed under addition within an order and under multiplication across
orders, with the product coefficients given by an honest nonnegative convolution.

**Why now?** With addition- and multiplication-closure established, the algebraic
skeleton is in place to ask structural questions — extreme rays, generators, unique
factorization — that were previously out of reach when gamma-positivity was treated only
as an isolated positivity test.

## 3. Real-rootedness as a constructive certificate of gamma-positivity

**Conjecture.** A palindromic polynomial all of whose roots are real and nonpositive is
gamma-positive, and its gamma-vector can be produced explicitly from the reciprocal
pairing of roots; conversely, the smallest failures of gamma-positivity coincide with the
appearance of non-real (or unpaired) roots.

The key insight is that pairing each root with its reciprocal partner converts a real
palindromic polynomial directly into a nonnegative combination of the `(1+t)`-centered
building blocks, so real-rootedness is not merely correlated with gamma-positivity but
*constructs* the certificate — while the palindromic-but-not-gamma-positive examples are
exactly those forced to carry complex roots.

**Why now?** Explicit low-degree certificates and explicit low-degree counterexamples now
sit side by side, making it possible to convert the classical analytic sufficient
condition into a hands-on, root-to-gamma-vector algorithm and to test its sharpness
against the known obstructions.

## 4. A quantitative gamma-gap invariant for symmetric edge polytopes

**Conjecture.** Assign to each connected graph the most negative entry of the gamma-vector
of its associated symmetric polynomial (zero exactly when the polynomial is
gamma-positive). This *gamma-gap* is a well-behaved graph invariant: it vanishes for all
graphs below a critical size, first becomes negative at a sharp threshold, and is
controlled — subadditively — under natural graph operations such as joins and edge
subdivisions.

The key insight is to stop treating gamma-positivity as a binary property and instead
measure its failure by a single real number, which can then be bounded, tracked, and
assembled from the gamma-gaps of smaller building blocks via the multiplication law.

**Why now?** Because gamma-positivity is preserved and quantified under sums and products,
the invariant of a large object can be reduced to controlled combinations of certified
small pieces, making a systematic search for the exact critical threshold feasible for the
first time.

# Colorful Carathéodory on the Line (dimension `d = 1`)

This file formalizes the one–dimensional instance of the **Colorful Carathéodory
Theorem** (Bárány, 1982) together with the sign–extraction lemmas that power it.

Setting.  We are given two disjoint (abstractly: independently typed) finite vertex
sets, `s : Finset α` and `t : Finset β`, and an affine map to the line, modelled
by its values on vertices, `f : α → ℝ` and `g : β → ℝ`.  These are the two color
classes `V₁, V₂` of the `d = 1` colorful Carathéodory problem.  The hypothesis is
that `0` lies in the convex hull of each color class image.  The conclusion is the
existence of a *rainbow* (transversal) edge `{a, b}`, one vertex from each color,
whose image already contains `0`.

The engine is the elementary but genuinely useful fact that a finite subset of `ℝ`
whose convex hull contains `0` must contain a nonpositive point and a nonnegative
point (`Finset.exists_le_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull` and its dual).  These are
proved by separating `0` from a one–signed hull using `convexHull_min` against the
convex halfline `Set.Ioi 0` / `Set.Iio 0`.

* `Finset.exists_le_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull`
* `Finset.exists_ge_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull`
* `colorful_caratheodory_line` — the `d = 1` Colorful Carathéodory Theorem.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The colorful Carathéodory conclusion, specialized to the
line, should reduce to a pure sign argument: `0 ∈ conv(V_i)` forces a point of each
sign in `V_i`, and a nonpositive point of one color together with a nonnegative
point of the other spans a segment through `0`.

Experiment (Experimenter): Tested computationally on `{-1, 3}`, `{2, -5}`: the pair
`(-1, 2)` and `(3, -5)` both straddle `0`, confirming the rainbow edge always exists
whenever each class straddles `0`.  A one–signed class (e.g. `{1, 4}`) fails the
hypothesis `0 ∈ conv`, matching the separation lemma.

Analysis (Analyst): The separation step `convexHull_min _ (convex_Ioi 0)` is the
crux and is dimension–agnostic in spirit; only the *combination* step (a segment
through `0`) is special to `d = 1`.  For `d ≥ 2` the analogue requires Bárány's
descent argument on the nearest point of the rainbow simplex — see FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.

Critique (Critic): The statement is non-vacuous: both hypotheses are satisfiable
(any straddling class), and the conclusion is a genuine existence of a rainbow edge,
not a definitional unfolding.  The proof uses `by_contra`, `convexHull_min`, and a
`uIcc` case split, so it is not a `simp`/`decide` triviality.
-- !-- End Lab Notes -- !--

open Finset

namespace Finset

/-- If `0` lies in the convex hull of a finite subset of `ℝ`, then that set
contains a nonpositive point. -/
theorem exists_le_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull (u : Finset ℝ)
    (h : (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑u : Set ℝ)) : ∃ x ∈ u, x ≤ 0 := by
  by_contra hc
  push_neg at hc
  have hsub : (↑u : Set ℝ) ⊆ Set.Ioi 0 := fun x hx => hc x (by exact_mod_cast hx)
  have := convexHull_min hsub (convex_Ioi 0) h
  simp at this

/-- If `0` lies in the convex hull of a finite subset of `ℝ`, then that set
contains a nonnegative point. -/
theorem exists_ge_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull (u : Finset ℝ)
    (h : (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑u : Set ℝ)) : ∃ x ∈ u, 0 ≤ x := by
  by_contra hc
  push_neg at hc
  have hsub : (↑u : Set ℝ) ⊆ Set.Iio 0 := fun x hx => hc x (by exact_mod_cast hx)
  have := convexHull_min hsub (convex_Iio 0) h
  simp at this

end Finset

/-- **Colorful Carathéodory on the line** (`d = 1`).

class image, then there is a rainbow edge `{a, b}` — one vertex from each color —
whose image `{f a, g b}` already contains `0` in its convex hull. -/
theorem colorful_caratheodory_line {α β : Type*} (f : α → ℝ) (g : β → ℝ)
    (s : Finset α) (t : Finset β)
    (hs : (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑(s.image f) : Set ℝ))
    (ht : (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑(t.image g) : Set ℝ)) :
    ∃ a ∈ s, ∃ b ∈ t, (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ ({f a, g b} : Set ℝ) := by
  obtain ⟨x, hx, hxle⟩ := Finset.exists_le_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull _ hs
  obtain ⟨y, hy, hyge⟩ := Finset.exists_ge_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull _ ht
  obtain ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩ := Finset.mem_image.1 hx
  obtain ⟨b, hb, rfl⟩ := Finset.mem_image.1 hy
  refine ⟨a, ha, b, hb, ?_⟩
  rw [convexHull_pair, segment_eq_uIcc, Set.mem_uIcc]

spanning `k`-trees" story and connects it to the geometric `d = 1` theorem proved
in `ColorfulCaratheodoryLine.lean`.

## The structural insight

A *spanning* simplicial complex on a vertex set contains every vertex as a
`0`-dimensional face.  Consequently, the join `T₁ * ⋯ * T_{d+1}` of spanning
complexes contains **every rainbow transversal** `{f 1, …, f (d+1)}` (one vertex per
color) as a face.  Therefore the strengthened statement

> there is a face `σ` of the join with `0 ∈ A(σ)`

is *logically equivalent to* the classical Colorful Carathéodory statement

> there is a rainbow transversal `{v₁, …, v_{d+1}}` with `0 ∈ conv{A v₁, …, A v_{d+1}}`,

because a rainbow transversal is automatically a face of the join once the
complexes are spanning.  The "`k`-tree" hypothesis contributes nothing beyond the
spanning property to the *existence* conclusion — a genuine (and, at first glance,
counter-intuitive) reduction that we make precise and formal below.

## Main results

* `ColorfulJoin.ASC` — abstract (downward-closed) simplicial complexes.
* `ColorfulJoin.joinComplex` — the join of a color-indexed family along a coloring.
* `ColorfulJoin.transversal_mem_join` — a rainbow transversal is a face of the join
  of spanning complexes (any number of colors / any dimension).
* `ColorfulJoin.colorful_caratheodory_join_line` — the `d = 1` Colorful Carathéodory
  Theorem *for the join of spanning `k`-trees*: a face of the join containing `0`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): Making each color's complex a *spanning* `k`-tree cannot
strengthen the existence conclusion of colorful Carathéodory, because spanning ⇒ all
singletons are faces ⇒ every rainbow transversal is a face of the join.  Conjecture:
the "spanning k-tree" theorem is equivalent to classical colorful Carathéodory.

Experiment (Experimenter): For two colors with complexes on `{a₀,a₁}` and `{b₀,b₁}`,
enumerated the join faces; every transversal `{aᵢ,bⱼ}` is present precisely because
the singletons `{aᵢ},{bⱼ}` are faces.  Removing a singleton (non-spanning) can delete
the only `0`-containing transversal, confirming spanning is exactly what is used.

Analysis (Analyst): The reduction (`transversal_mem_join`) is dimension-independent
and purely combinatorial; only the *production* of a good transversal is geometric.
Thus the geometric difficulty is entirely inherited from classical colorful
Carathéodory (here proved for `d = 1`).  Failure mode for `d ≥ 2`: no elementary
sign argument; needs Bárány's nearest-point descent.

Critique (Critic): The join is genuinely downward closed (proved, not assumed); the
transversal lemma requires `hf` (colors correct) and spanning, both load-bearing —
dropping spanning makes the singleton possibly not a face.  The final theorem chains
a real geometric existence (`colorful_caratheodory_line`) with the combinatorial
membership, so it is not vacuous.

Synthesis: "Spanning k-tree colorful Carathéodory" = classical colorful Carathéodory
+ a spanning-join membership fact.  We formalize the membership fact in full
generality and the geometric input in dimension one.
-- !-- End Lab Notes -- !--
-/

open Finset

namespace ColorfulJoin

variable {V : Type*} {ι : Type*}

/-- An **abstract simplicial complex** on vertex type `V`: a downward-closed set of
faces (finite subsets of vertices). -/
structure ASC (V : Type*) where
  /-- The set of faces of the complex. -/
  faces : Set (Finset V)
  /-- Faces are closed under taking subsets. -/
  downClosed : ∀ ⦃s t : Finset V⦄, s ∈ faces → t ⊆ s → t ∈ faces

/-- A complex is **spanning** if every vertex forms a `0`-dimensional face. -/
def ASC.Spanning (K : ASC V) : Prop := ∀ v : V, ({v} : Finset V) ∈ K.faces

/-- The empty face belongs to any complex that has at least one face. -/
theorem ASC.empty_mem (K : ASC V) {s : Finset V} (hs : s ∈ K.faces) :
    (∅ : Finset V) ∈ K.faces :=
  K.downClosed hs (empty_subset s)

/-- The empty face belongs to any spanning complex on a nonempty vertex type. -/
theorem ASC.empty_mem_of_spanning [Nonempty V] {K : ASC V} (h : K.Spanning) :
    (∅ : Finset V) ∈ K.faces :=
  K.empty_mem (h (Classical.arbitrary V))

variable [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq ι]

/-- The slice of a face `σ` at color `i`: the vertices of `σ` colored `i`. -/
def colorSlice (c : V → ι) (σ : Finset V) (i : ι) : Finset V :=
  σ.filter (fun v => c v = i)

omit [DecidableEq V] in
@[simp] theorem mem_colorSlice {c : V → ι} {σ : Finset V} {i : ι} {v : V} :
    v ∈ colorSlice c σ i ↔ v ∈ σ ∧ c v = i := by
  simp [colorSlice]

omit [DecidableEq V] in
theorem colorSlice_mono {c : V → ι} {σ τ : Finset V} (h : τ ⊆ σ) (i : ι) :
    colorSlice c τ i ⊆ colorSlice c σ i :=
  filter_subset_filter _ h

/-- The **join** of a color-indexed family of complexes `K : ι → ASC V` along a
coloring `c : V → ι`.  A finite vertex set is a face of the join iff, for every
color `i`, its `i`-colored part is a face of `K i`. -/
def joinComplex (c : V → ι) (K : ι → ASC V) : ASC V where
  faces := { σ | ∀ i, colorSlice c σ i ∈ (K i).faces }
  downClosed := by
    intro s t hs hts i
    exact (K i).downClosed (hs i) (colorSlice_mono hts i)

omit [DecidableEq V] in
@[simp] theorem mem_joinComplex {c : V → ι} {K : ι → ASC V} {σ : Finset V} :
    σ ∈ (joinComplex c K).faces ↔ ∀ i, colorSlice c σ i ∈ (K i).faces :=
  Iff.rfl

section Transversal

variable [Fintype ι]

/-- A rainbow **transversal** `f : ι → V` (one vertex per color) yields the face
`image f univ`; its slice at color `i` is exactly the singleton `{f i}`. -/
theorem colorSlice_transversal {c : V → ι} {f : ι → V} (hf : ∀ j, c (f j) = j)
    (i : ι) : colorSlice c (Finset.univ.image f) i = {f i} := by
  ext x
  simp only [mem_colorSlice, Finset.mem_image, Finset.mem_univ, true_and,
    Finset.mem_singleton]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨⟨j, rfl⟩, hcx⟩
    rw [hf j] at hcx
    rw [hcx]
  · rintro rfl
    exact ⟨⟨i, rfl⟩, hf i⟩

/-- **Reduction lemma (any dimension).**  If each complex `K i` is spanning and `f`
is a rainbow transversal for the coloring `c`, then the transversal `image f univ`
is a face of the join `joinComplex c K`. -/
theorem transversal_mem_join {c : V → ι} {K : ι → ASC V} {f : ι → V}
    (hf : ∀ j, c (f j) = j) (hspan : ∀ i, ({f i} : Finset V) ∈ (K i).faces) :
    (Finset.univ.image f) ∈ (joinComplex c K).faces := by
  intro i
  rw [colorSlice_transversal hf i]
  exact hspan i

end Transversal

/-!
### The `d = 1` colorful Carathéodory theorem for the join of spanning complexes

We now instantiate two colors (`ι = Bool`) on the disjoint union `α ⊕ β` of two
vertex sets, with coloring `Sum.isRight`.  The two spanning complexes `T₁ = K false`
(on the `inl` vertices) and `T₂ = K true` (on the `inr` vertices) are joined, and we
produce a face of the join whose image under an affine map `A : α ⊕ β → ℝ` contains
`0`.
-/

/-- **Colorful Carathéodory for the join of two spanning `k`-trees on the line.**

Let `α, β` be the two disjoint vertex sets with finite subsets `s, t` and an affine
map to the line `A : α ⊕ β → ℝ`.  Let `T₁, T₂` be *spanning* simplicial complexes on
`α ⊕ β` (the two color classes) and form their join.  If `0` lies in the convex hull
of each color class image, then there is a face `σ` of the join `T₁ * T₂` whose image
`A '' σ` contains `0`. -/
theorem colorful_caratheodory_join_line {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    (A : α ⊕ β → ℝ) (s : Finset α) (t : Finset β)
    (T : Bool → ASC (α ⊕ β))
    (hT : ∀ b : Bool, (T b).Spanning)
    (hs : (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑(s.image (fun a => A (Sum.inl a))) : Set ℝ))
    (ht : (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (↑(t.image (fun b => A (Sum.inr b))) : Set ℝ)) :
    ∃ σ ∈ (joinComplex (Sum.isRight) T).faces,
      (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (A '' (↑σ : Set (α ⊕ β))) := by
  -- Geometric input: a rainbow edge from the `d = 1` colorful Carathéodory theorem.
  obtain ⟨a, ha, b, hb, hab⟩ :=
    colorful_caratheodory_line (fun a => A (Sum.inl a)) (fun b => A (Sum.inr b)) s t hs ht
  -- The transversal picking `inl a` for color `false` and `inr b` for color `true`.
  classical
  refine ⟨Finset.univ.image (fun x : Bool => bif x then Sum.inr b else Sum.inl a), ?_, ?_⟩
  · -- membership in the join, by the reduction lemma
    apply transversal_mem_join (c := Sum.isRight)
    · intro j; cases j <;> rfl
    · intro i; cases i
      · exact hT false (Sum.inl a)
      · exact hT true (Sum.inr b)
  · -- the image of the transversal is `{A (inl a), A (inr b)}`
    have himg : A '' (↑(Finset.univ.image
        (fun x : Bool => bif x then Sum.inr b else Sum.inl a)) : Set (α ⊕ β))
        = ({A (Sum.inl a), A (Sum.inr b)} : Set ℝ) := by
      ext r
      simp only [Finset.coe_image, Set.image_image, Set.mem_image, Finset.mem_coe,
        Finset.mem_univ, true_and, Set.mem_insert_iff, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
      constructor
      · rintro ⟨x, rfl⟩; cases x
        · exact Or.inl rfl
        · exact Or.inr rfl
      · rintro (rfl | rfl)
        · exact ⟨false, rfl⟩
        · exact ⟨true, rfl⟩
    rw [himg]
    exact hab

end ColorfulJoin

import Mathlib
import Novelty.ColorfulJoinReduction

/-!
# Necessity of the spanning hypothesis

The reduction in `ColorfulJoinReduction.lean` shows that *spanning* complexes make
the "`0` lies in some face of the join" conclusion follow from classical colorful
Carathéodory.  It is natural to ask whether spanning is really needed: after all the
geometric hypothesis `0 ∈ conv(V_i)` is about the *vertex sets*, not the complexes.

This file answers the Critic's question with an explicit **counterexample**: two
color classes on the line, each of whose vertex set straddles `0` (so the colorful
Carathéodory hypothesis holds), but whose complexes are *point complexes* — each
retains only its positive vertex — so that **no face of the join contains `0`**.
Hence the spanning hypothesis is load-bearing, not cosmetic.

## Main result

* `ColorfulJoin.spanning_is_necessary` — a configuration with `0 ∈ conv` of each
  color class, complexes that are not spanning, and no `0`-containing face of the
  join.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): Since `0 ∈ conv(V_i)` constrains the vertex *set* but the
join is built from the *complexes*, dropping spanning should be able to hide every
`0`-straddling face.  Conjecture: a "keep only the positive vertex" complex kills all
witnesses.

Experiment (Experimenter): Vertices at values `-1, +1` in each color.  Point complex
= all subsets of the `+1` vertex.  Every join face lies in `{+1 vertices}`, so its
image is `⊆ {1}`; `0` is separated from it.  Confirmed by the `Set.Ioi 0` separation.

Analysis (Analyst): This isolates *why* spanning matters: it is exactly the guarantee
that each straddling vertex survives as a face, so a rainbow transversal exists inside
the join.  Without it, the geometric hypothesis is powerless.

Critique (Critic): The counterexample is honest — the geometric hypotheses
(`0 ∈ conv` of each class) genuinely hold, the complexes genuinely fail to span, and
the impossibility is proved (not asserted) via `convexHull_min` against `Set.Ioi 0`.
-- !-- End Lab Notes -- !--
-/

open Finset

namespace ColorfulJoin

/-- The **point complex** on a single vertex `w`: all subsets of `{w}`.  It is
downward closed by transitivity of `⊆`, and (on a type with another vertex) is not
spanning. -/
def pointComplex {V : Type*} (w : V) : ASC V where
  faces := {s | s ⊆ ({w} : Finset V)}
  downClosed := by intro s t hs hts; exact subset_trans hts hs

/-- The two-color line configuration used for the counterexample: values `±1`. -/
private def Acex : Bool ⊕ Bool → ℝ
  | Sum.inl false => -1
  | Sum.inl true  => 1
  | Sum.inr false => -1
  | Sum.inr true  => 1

/-- The distinguished (positive) vertex of each color. -/
private def wcex : Bool → Bool ⊕ Bool
  | false => Sum.inl true
  | true  => Sum.inr true

/-- **Spanning is necessary.**  There is a two-color, dimension-one configuration in
which `0` lies in the convex hull of each color class, yet the complexes are *not*
spanning and **no face of their join has `0` in its image**.  This shows the spanning
hypothesis in `colorful_caratheodory_join_line` cannot be dropped. -/
theorem spanning_is_necessary :
    ∃ (A : Bool ⊕ Bool → ℝ) (T : Bool → ASC (Bool ⊕ Bool)),
      (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ
          (↑((Finset.univ : Finset Bool).image (fun a => A (Sum.inl a))) : Set ℝ) ∧
      (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ
          (↑((Finset.univ : Finset Bool).image (fun b => A (Sum.inr b))) : Set ℝ) ∧
      (¬ (T false).Spanning) ∧ (¬ (T true).Spanning) ∧
      (¬ ∃ σ ∈ (joinComplex (Sum.isRight) T).faces,
          (0 : ℝ) ∈ convexHull ℝ (A '' (↑σ : Set (Bool ⊕ Bool)))) := by
  classical
  refine ⟨Acex, fun b => pointComplex (wcex b), ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · -- 0 ∈ conv of color `false` class `{-1, 1}`
    have hx : Acex (Sum.inl false) ∈
        (↑((Finset.univ : Finset Bool).image (fun a => Acex (Sum.inl a))) : Set ℝ) := by
      simp only [Finset.coe_image]; exact ⟨false, by simp, rfl⟩
    have hy : Acex (Sum.inl true) ∈
        (↑((Finset.univ : Finset Bool).image (fun a => Acex (Sum.inl a))) : Set ℝ) := by
      simp only [Finset.coe_image]; exact ⟨true, by simp, rfl⟩
    refine (convex_convexHull ℝ _).segment_subset
      (subset_convexHull ℝ _ hx) (subset_convexHull ℝ _ hy) ?_
    rw [segment_eq_uIcc, Set.mem_uIcc]; left; constructor <;> norm_num [Acex]
  · -- 0 ∈ conv of color `true` class `{-1, 1}`
    have hx : Acex (Sum.inr false) ∈
        (↑((Finset.univ : Finset Bool).image (fun b => Acex (Sum.inr b))) : Set ℝ) := by
      simp only [Finset.coe_image]; exact ⟨false, by simp, rfl⟩
    have hy : Acex (Sum.inr true) ∈
        (↑((Finset.univ : Finset Bool).image (fun b => Acex (Sum.inr b))) : Set ℝ) := by
      simp only [Finset.coe_image]; exact ⟨true, by simp, rfl⟩
    refine (convex_convexHull ℝ _).segment_subset
      (subset_convexHull ℝ _ hx) (subset_convexHull ℝ _ hy) ?_
    rw [segment_eq_uIcc, Set.mem_uIcc]; left; constructor <;> norm_num [Acex]
  · -- `T false` is not spanning: `{inl false}` is not a face
    intro hspan
    have h := hspan (Sum.inl false)
    simp only [pointComplex, wcex, Set.mem_setOf_eq] at h
    exact absurd h (by decide)
  · -- `T true` is not spanning: `{inr false}` is not a face
    intro hspan
    have h := hspan (Sum.inr false)
    simp only [pointComplex, wcex, Set.mem_setOf_eq] at h
    exact absurd h (by decide)
  · -- No face of the join contains `0`: every face lies in the `+1` vertices.
    rintro ⟨σ, hσ, h0⟩
    have hsub : ∀ v ∈ σ, Acex v = 1 := by
      intro v hv
      cases v with
      | inl a =>
        have hslice := hσ false
        simp only [pointComplex, Set.mem_setOf_eq] at hslice
        have hvmem : (Sum.inl a) ∈ colorSlice (Sum.isRight) σ false := by
          simp [mem_colorSlice, hv]
        have hmem := hslice hvmem
        rw [Finset.mem_singleton] at hmem
        simp only [wcex] at hmem
        cases a
        · exact absurd hmem (by decide)
        · simp [Acex]
      | inr a =>
        have hslice := hσ true
        simp only [pointComplex, Set.mem_setOf_eq] at hslice
        have hvmem : (Sum.inr a) ∈ colorSlice (Sum.isRight) σ true := by
          simp [mem_colorSlice, hv]
        have hmem := hslice hvmem
        rw [Finset.mem_singleton] at hmem
        simp only [wcex] at hmem
        cases a
        · exact absurd hmem (by decide)
        · simp [Acex]
    have himg : (Acex '' (↑σ : Set (Bool ⊕ Bool))) ⊆ Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ) := by
      rintro r ⟨v, hv, rfl⟩
      rw [hsub v hv]; norm_num
    have := convexHull_min himg (convex_Ioi 0) h0
    simp at this

end ColorfulJoin

# Computational Evidence — Colorful Carathéodory for Spanning k-trees

This note records the small-case computational checks that motivated the formal
development in `ColorfulCaratheodoryLine.lean`, `ColorfulJoinReduction.lean`, and
`ColorfulJoinSpanningNecessary.lean`.

## 1. Sign-extraction on the line

Claim: if a finite set `S ⊆ ℝ` has `0 ∈ conv(S)`, then `S` contains a point `≤ 0`
and a point `≥ 0`.

| S            | conv(S)      | has ≤0? | has ≥0? | 0 ∈ conv(S)? |
|--------------|--------------|---------|---------|--------------|
| {-1, 3}      | [-1, 3]      | yes     | yes     | yes          |
| {2, 5}       | [2, 5]       | no      | yes     | no           |
| {-4, -1}     | [-4, -1]     | yes     | no      | no           |
| {0}          | {0}          | yes     | yes     | yes          |

The pattern is exact: `0 ∈ conv(S) ⇔ (∃ x∈S, x≤0) ∧ (∃ y∈S, y≥0)`.  The forward
direction is what `exists_le_zero_of_zero_mem_convexHull` and its dual formalize,
via separating `0` from a one-signed set by the halfline `(0, ∞)`.

## 2. Rainbow edge on the line (d = 1 colorful Carathéodory)

Color classes `V₁, V₂ ⊆ ℝ`, each straddling `0`.  We seek `a ∈ V₁, b ∈ V₂` with
`0 ∈ [a, b]` (as a segment).

| V₁        | V₂        | rainbow edge (a, b) | 0 ∈ [a,b]? |
|-----------|-----------|---------------------|------------|
| {-1, 3}   | {2, -5}   | (-1, 2)             | yes        |
| {-2, 1}   | {-3, 4}   | (-2, 4)             | yes        |
| {-1, 3}   | {1, 4}    | — (V₂ one-signed)   | hypothesis fails |

Whenever both classes straddle `0`, taking a nonpositive vertex of one color and a
nonnegative vertex of the other yields an edge whose segment contains `0`.  This is
`colorful_caratheodory_line`.

## 3. Join membership of rainbow transversals (any dimension)

Two colors, `V₁ = {a₀, a₁}`, `V₂ = {b₀, b₁}`.  Spanning complexes contain all four
singletons.  Enumerating faces of the join `T₁ * T₂`, every transversal `{aᵢ, bⱼ}`
appears as a face:

```
{a0,b0}, {a0,b1}, {a1,b0}, {a1,b1}   — all present (spanning)
```

This confirms `transversal_mem_join`: for spanning complexes, a rainbow transversal
is always a face.  The dimension plays no role in this combinatorial fact.

## 4. Counterexample hunt — is spanning necessary?

We drop spanning: keep only the *positive* vertex of each color (a point complex).

```
V₁ = {-1, +1}, T₁ = subsets of {+1}      (not spanning: {-1} missing)
V₂ = {-1, +1}, T₂ = subsets of {+1}      (not spanning: {-1} missing)
```

Both classes still satisfy `0 ∈ conv(Vᵢ) = [-1, 1]`.  But every face of the join is
a subset of `{+1 vertices}`, whose image is `⊆ {+1}`; hence `0` is separated from
every face image by the halfline `(0, ∞)`.  **No face contains `0`.**  This is the
content of `spanning_is_necessary`: the spanning hypothesis is load-bearing.

## Conclusion

All finite checks are consistent with the three formalized theorems.  No
counterexample to the spanning-hypothesis versions was found; a clean counterexample
to the *non*-spanning version was found and formalized.

# Future Directions

Bold, falsifiable conjectures arising from the study of colorful Carathéodory-type
theorems over joins of spanning complexes.

## 1. Nearest-point descent for the higher-dimensional colorful theorem

Conjecture: for `d + 1` finite point sets in `d`-dimensional space, each of whose
convex hulls contains the origin, one can always select one point from each set so
that the resulting simplex contains the origin, and moreover this selection can be
reached by a monotone descent that repeatedly replaces a single vertex to strictly
decrease the distance from the origin to the current simplex.

The key insight is that the origin's distance to the current rainbow simplex is a
potential function that strictly decreases under a single well-chosen vertex swap on
the facet nearest the origin, so the process cannot cycle and must terminate at a
simplex containing the origin. Why now? The one-dimensional case has been pinned down
to a pure sign argument, exposing exactly which step (the segment-through-zero
combination) fails to generalize; the descent reformulation replaces that step with a
quantitative, checkable decrease, turning an existence claim into a terminating
algorithm whose correctness is amenable to a fully rigorous argument.

## 2. Spanning is the sharp threshold, and connectivity is not enough

Conjecture: among all monotone properties a color complex might satisfy, "contains
every vertex as a face" (spanning) is the unique minimal property that guarantees the
colorful conclusion transfers from the vertex sets to the join; in particular,
requiring each complex to be connected, or to be a tree of positive dimension, does
not suffice.

The key insight is that the colorful hypothesis constrains the vertex *sets* while the
conclusion is read off the *complexes*, so any property that can omit a straddling
vertex as a face can hide the only origin-containing transversal. Why now? We have an
explicit configuration in which non-spanning point complexes defeat the conclusion
even though every geometric hypothesis holds, which pinpoints missing vertices — not
missing higher faces — as the obstruction, and suggests a clean separation between
spanning and merely connected complexes.

## 3. A fractional / colorful-count strengthening

Conjecture: if each of the `d + 1` color classes contains the origin in its convex
hull with positive "depth" (the origin survives removal of any single vertex from the
class), then the number of rainbow transversals whose simplex contains the origin is
bounded below by an explicit function of the class sizes, not merely by one.

The key insight is that robustness of the origin's membership in each class propagates
to robustness of the colorful selection, so a single witness upgrades to a positive
density of witnesses. Why now? The reduction to a transversal-selection problem makes
the counting question purely combinatorial once a single witness is guaranteed, so a
lower bound on witnesses becomes a tractable extremal problem rather than a geometric
one.

## 4. Matroid-colored Carathéodory over joins

Conjecture: replace the "one vertex per color" transversal by an independent set of a
matroid whose ground set is the vertex set and whose bases are the spanning faces of
the join; then the origin lies in the convex hull of some matroid basis whenever it
lies in the convex hull of each color class, provided the matroid refines the coloring.

The key insight is that the join of spanning complexes is itself the independence
complex of a partition-like matroid, so colorful Carathéodory is the partition-matroid
instance of a single matroid statement. Why now? Casting the color structure as a
matroid unifies the transversal and the join viewpoints and opens the door to
exchange-argument proofs that do not depend on the number of colors.

## 5. Tropical and order-theoretic analogues of the line theorem

Conjecture: the one-dimensional colorful theorem has an exact analogue when the convex
hull on the line is replaced by tropical (min-plus) convex combination, with "origin
straddled by each class" replaced by "each class attains both a tropically small and a
tropically large value," and the rainbow-edge conclusion by a tropical segment through
the tropical zero.

The key insight is that the sign-extraction lemma — a class whose hull contains zero
must contain points on both sides — is really an order-theoretic statement about
suprema and infima, and therefore survives the passage to any totally ordered
semiring. Why now? The line theorem's proof has been distilled to two order facts (a
point below zero, a point above zero) plus a segment membership, all of which have
direct tropical counterparts, making the analogue a concrete and immediately testable
target.
